lead: Two shops can sell the same average number of cups of tea each day and still feel very different. One sells almost the same count daily; the other swings from very few to very many. The mean from 1.2 gives the centre but hides this swing. A measure of dispersion states how far the values sit from that centre, in marks, rupees or standard units. Range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation do this job. They drive quality control, exam result checks, stock risk and weather warnings.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for the mean and median that act as the centre, and 1.1 for frequency tables.

blocks.text: Range is the gap between the largest and smallest value. For a list x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ sorted ascending, R = L − S, where L is the largest value and S is the smallest. The coefficient of range removes units: (L − S)/(L + S). For a continuous series, L is the upper limit of the highest class and S is the lower limit of the lowest class. The range uses only two values, so one outlier can change it.
R = L − S, coefficient of range = (L − S)/(L + S)
blocks.where: L is the largest value, S is the smallest value, and R is the range in the same unit as the data.

blocks.text: Quartile deviation splits the data at the first quartile Q₁ and third quartile Q₃. Q₁ is the value below which one quarter of the data lies; Q₃ is the value below which three quarters lie. QD = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2. Its coefficient is (Q₃ − Q₁)/(Q₃ + Q₁). For an individual series with n items in order, Q₁ is the ((n + 1)/4)th item and Q₃ is the (3(n + 1)/4)th item. For discrete and continuous series, locate these positions in the cumulative frequency column and read the value or interpolate in the class.
QD = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2, coefficient of QD = (Q₃ − Q₁)/(Q₃ + Q₁)
blocks.where: Q₁ is the first quartile, Q₃ is the third quartile, and QD is the quartile deviation in the data's unit.

blocks.text: QD is small when the middle half is packed tightly. It ignores the lowest quarter and highest quarter, so extreme marks do not dominate it.

sections.h3: Mean deviation about mean and median

blocks.text: Mean deviation measures the average distance of each value from a chosen centre A. Use absolute distances, because signed deviations from the mean add to zero, and in any case positive and negative deviations would cancel each other. For an individual series, MD = (Σ|xᵢ − A|)/n, where xᵢ is each value, A is the centre, n is the number of values, and the bars mean absolute value. For a discrete series, MD = (Σfᵢ|xᵢ − A|)/N, where fᵢ is the frequency of xᵢ and N = Σfᵢ. For a continuous series, replace each class by its class mark mᵢ, the midpoint of the class, and use MD = (Σfᵢ|mᵢ − A|)/N.
MD = Σ|xᵢ − A|/n (individual), MD = Σfᵢ|xᵢ − A|/N (discrete)
blocks.where: A is the chosen centre, n is the number of values, fᵢ is a frequency, N = Σfᵢ, and | | means absolute value.

blocks.text: A is usually the mean x̄ or the median. The coefficient is MD/A, using the same A. Steps: find the centre; write each absolute deviation; multiply by frequency where frequencies exist; add; divide by n or N. Mean deviation about the median is never larger than mean deviation about the mean for the same data. It uses every value but treats a deviation of 2 and a deviation of 20 in direct proportion, unlike SD which squares them.

items: Choose the centre A: the mean x̄ or the median.
Write the absolute deviation |xᵢ − A| for each value.
Multiply by frequency fᵢ when a frequency table is given.
Add all products and divide by n or N.

blocks.text: Standard deviation is the square root of the average squared distance from the mean. For a population of n values, σ = √(Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n), where σ is the standard deviation, xᵢ is each value, x̄ is the mean, and n is the number of values. Variance is σ². For a discrete series, σ = √(Σfᵢxᵢ²/N − (Σfᵢxᵢ/N)²), with fᵢ the frequency, xᵢ the value, and N = Σfᵢ. For a continuous series, xᵢ is the class mark mᵢ. The second term is the square of the mean.

blocks.where: σ is the standard deviation, fᵢ is a frequency, xᵢ is a value or class mark, and N = Σfᵢ.

blocks.text: Direct method uses the formula above. Assumed-mean method takes a trial value A, writes dᵢ = xᵢ − A, and uses σ = √(Σfᵢdᵢ²/N − (Σfᵢdᵢ/N)²). Step-deviation method takes dᵢ = (xᵢ − A)/h, where h is the class width, then σ = h × √(Σfᵢdᵢ²/N − (Σfᵢdᵢ/N)²). These two methods only reduce arithmetic; the answer is the same.

blocks.where: A is the assumed mean, h is the class width, fᵢ is a frequency, and N = Σfᵢ.

blocks.text: Properties: adding a constant c to every value leaves σ unchanged, because all distances from the new mean are the same. Multiplying every value by a constant a multiplies σ by |a| and variance by a². Always variance = mean of squares − square of mean. For two groups of sizes n₁ and n₂, means x̄₁ and x̄₂, standard deviations σ₁ and σ₂, the combined mean is x̄ = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂). The combined variance is [n₁(σ₁² + d₁²) + n₂(σ₂² + d₂²)]/(n₁ + n₂), where d₁ = x̄₁ − x̄ and d₂ = x̄₂ − x̄.
For a normal distribution only, QD = 0.6745σ. This links the middle-half spread to the standard deviation when the curve is bell-shaped.

figure.caption: Two frequency curves with the same centre at 5; the taller, narrower curve belongs to the data with the smaller standard deviation.

spec.aria: Two bell-shaped curves with the same centre at 5, one tall and narrow and one short and wide.

examples.question: The runs scored by a batter in 7 innings are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Find the range and its coefficient, the quartile deviation and its coefficient, the mean deviation about the mean, and the standard deviation.
steps: The data are already in ascending order. n = 7. Sum = 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 14 = 56. Mean x̄ = 56/7 = 8 runs.
Range R = L − S = 14 − 2 = 12 runs. Coefficient of range = (L − S)/(L + S) = 12/16 = 0.75.
Q₁ position = (n + 1)/4 = 8/4 = 2nd item = 4 runs. Q₃ position = 3(n + 1)/4 = 24/4 = 6th item = 12 runs. QD = (12 − 4)/2 = 4 runs. Coefficient of QD = (12 − 4)/(12 + 4) = 8/16 = 0.5.
Absolute deviations from the mean: |2 − 8| = 6, |4 − 8| = 4, |6 − 8| = 2, |8 − 8| = 0, |10 − 8| = 2, |12 − 8| = 4, |14 − 8| = 6. Sum = 24. MD about mean = 24/7 = 3.43 runs (2 decimal places).
Squares: 4, 16, 36, 64, 100, 144, 196. Sum = 560. Mean of squares = 560/7 = 80. Variance = 80 − 8² = 80 − 64 = 16 runs². Standard deviation = √16 = 4 runs.
examples.answer: Range = 12 runs, coefficient of range = 0.75; QD = 4 runs, coefficient of QD = 0.5; mean deviation about mean = 3.43 runs; variance = 16 runs² and standard deviation = 4 runs.
examples.check:
data = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]
n = len(data)
mean = sum(data) / n
R = max(data) - min(data)
coefR = R / (max(data) + min(data))
Q1 = data[1]
Q3 = data[5]
QD = (Q3 - Q1) / 2
coefQD = (Q3 - Q1) / (Q3 + Q1)
MD = sum(abs(x - mean) for x in data) / n
var = sum(x * x for x in data) / n - mean * mean
sd = var ** 0.5
print(R)
print(coefR)
print(QD)
print(coefQD)
print(round(MD, 2))
print(round(var, 2))
print(round(sd, 2))

traps: For a continuous series, take deviations from class marks, never from class limits. Using limits changes the mean and the standard deviation.
Coefficient of range uses (L + S) in the denominator, and coefficient of QD uses (Q₃ + Q₁). Do not put the mean there.
Mean deviation needs absolute deviations. If you drop the absolute value, the signed deviations from the mean add to zero.
Dividing by n gives the population standard deviation used in descriptive work; dividing by n − 1 gives the sample value. Mixing the two changes the answer.
QD = 0.6745σ holds only for a normal distribution. It is not a general formula for every data set.

quiz.q: Define range and its coefficient for an individual series.
quiz.a: Range R = L − S, where L is the largest value and S is the smallest value. Coefficient of range = (L − S)/(L + S).

quiz.q: Why is quartile deviation less affected by extreme values than range?
quiz.a: QD uses Q₁ and Q₃, which cut off the lowest and highest quarters. A single very large value can change the range but does not enter the middle half unless it crosses Q₃.

quiz.q: For the data 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, find Q₁, Q₃, the quartile deviation and its coefficient.
Group 1 has n₁ = 30, mean 60, SD 8. Group 2 has n₂ = 20, mean 50, SD 6. Find the combined standard deviation.
Every value in a data set is multiplied by −2. What happens to the standard deviation and the variance?
quiz.a: The standard deviation is multiplied by |−2| = 2. The variance is multiplied by (−2)² = 4.

quiz.q: Why does mean deviation use absolute deviations from the centre?
quiz.a: Signed deviations from the mean add to zero, so their average would always be zero. Absolute values measure distance without sign and give a positive spread.

quiz.q: A normal distribution has standard deviation σ = 10. Find its quartile deviation.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, control charts plot a process mean with limits at ±3σ, so a small SD means tight quality and a large SD warns of trouble. In finance, σ of daily returns is called volatility and feeds directly into risk models. Robust versions replace the mean and SD with the median and the median absolute deviation when outliers are common. Search next for interquartile range, median absolute deviation, root mean square error and variance-stabilizing transformations.
